routes.description: Establish that Christian belief can remain rational when treated as an evidence-sensitive cumulative worldview whose historical, textual, philosophical, and moral components are assessed together rather than as isolated claims requiring certainty.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supplies a coherent evidential account of faith, a cumulative basis for the resurrection and Christian distinctiveness, a qualified model of scriptural reliability, and morally relevant explanations of hiddenness, judgment, and sincere nonbelief.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined Christian account has sufficient evidential and explanatory support to remain rationally sustainable amid the specified skeptical challenges.

centralBridges.description: Define faith as evidence-grounded trust under uncertainty and explain why contrary possibilities do not by themselves make that trust irrational.
Provide a cumulative historical case for resurrection that compares testimony, textual reliability, relevant historical considerations, and alternative explanations.
Defend a model in which culturally situated, composite, and fallible human transmission can still preserve evidentially and theologically relevant scriptural meaning.
Explain why limited divine disclosure and present religious commitment can serve moral transformation while judgment remains compatible with sincere evidential limitations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show how qualified historical claims about the Exodus and Jesus can survive objections based on archaeology, ancient conventions, and literary dependence.
Distinguish Christianity from rival traditions and alleged parallels through case-specific comparison rather than assuming either uniqueness or parity.

routes.description: Establish that withholding Christian belief is rational because the available disclosure, testimony, textual record, historical support, and moral account do not adequately distinguish Christianity from naturalistic explanations or competing traditions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if ordinary evidential expectations, sincere nonbelief, scriptural development, historical uncertainty, religious diversity, and alternative explanations jointly undercut the warrant claimed for distinctively Christian conclusions.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available evidence does not sufficiently distinguish Christian supernatural claims from error, cultural development, or rival religious claims.

centralBridges.description: Argue that evidence-based belief requires clearer disclosure than sincere nonbelievers presently receive and that biblical models do not resolve this disparity.
Show why ancient resurrection testimony and related historical claims require stronger support before overcoming ordinary experience and alternative explanations.
Explain how textual variation, internal diversity, literary reuse, discrepancies, and culturally situated authorship weaken claims of reliable divine communication.
Press whether hell, postmortem opportunity, and the asserted present necessity of belief coherently address sincere skepticism and limited evidence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use population, archaeological, and interpretive difficulties in the Exodus traditions to test their historical and religious evidential force.
Use competing religions, recurring supernatural motifs, and naturalistic accounts of religious experience to challenge Christian epistemic privilege.

sections.title: Evidential Faith, Divine Hiddenness, and Adequate Disclosure
sections.rationale: This issue tests the governing conception of rational faith and whether testimonial or prior evidence can justify trust when sincere nonbelievers lack the clearer disclosure they regard as necessary.

sections.title: Hell, Sincere Nonbelief, and the Present Value of Commitment
sections.rationale: This issue bears on whether Christian belief offers a coherent moral account of judgment, freely chosen separation, postmortem recognition, and the significance of commitment during earthly life.

sections.title: Resurrection Testimony and Cumulative Historical Evidence
sections.rationale: The resurrection is a central distinctively Christian claim, making the adequacy of testimony, burial and empty-tomb considerations, document reliability, ordinary expectations, and rival explanations indispensable.

sections.title: Biblical Reliability, Human Composition, and Literary Development
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether textual variants, discrepancies, composite authorship, apostolic disagreement, and literary reuse are compatible with scripture functioning as reliable evidence and divine communication.

sections.title: Exodus Historicity, Archaeology, and Ancient Conventions
sections.rationale: The dispute over a minimal migration, population figures, conquest traditions, archaeological absence, and ancient numerical conventions provides a focused test of biblical historical reasoning.

sections.title: Religious Pluralism, Ancient Parallels, and Religious Experience
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether Christianity can be non-question-beggingly distinguished from rival scriptures, recurring supernatural traditions, alleged literary parallels, and naturalistic explanations of spiritual experience.
